summary: This RFC extends IKEv2 for group key management, following the MSEC architecture with member registration and group rekeying. It obsoletes RFC 6407.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of devices that all send and receive the same multicast traffic has to share one encryption key, and that key has to be replaced from time to time without leaving a removed member able to read the traffic. This document defines that mechanism as an extension to IKEv2, the protocol used to set up secure IP connections. It covers how a device joins the group, how it is given the shared key, and how the key is later replaced.

questions: how does ipsec multicast group key management work
subtitle: An extension to IKEv2 that hands a shared encryption key to a group of devices and replaces it later.

tldr.problem: A group of devices that all send and receive the same multicast traffic needs one shared IPsec key, and that key has to be replaced from time to time without leaving a removed member able to read the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: G-IKEv2 adds two exchanges to IKEv2. A member registers with the Group Controller/Key Server and receives the group policy and keys, and later the server rekeys the group, either by one multicast message or by a separate exchange with each member.
tldr.outcome: The document registers four new IKEv2 payloads, four new exchange types and the registries behind them. It replaces the Group Domain of Interpretation, which did the same job with IKEv1.

today: RFC 9838 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 6407, the Group Domain of Interpretation, which did the same job with IKEv1. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Group Key Management Is For
sections.content:
This document presents an extension to IKEv2 called G-IKEv2, which accommodates group key management. A group key management protocol provides IPsec keys and policy to a set of IPsec devices that are authorized to communicate using a Group Security Association defined in the Multicast Group Security Architecture. The data communications within the group, for example IP multicast packets, are protected by a key pushed to the group members by the Group Controller/Key Server.

G-IKEv2 conforms to the Multicast Group Security Architecture, the multicast extensions to the IPsec architecture, and the MSEC Group Key Management Architecture. It replaces the Group Domain of Interpretation, which defines a similar group key management protocol using IKEv1. Group key management use cases can benefit from the simplicity, increased robustness and cryptographic improvements of IKEv2.

G-IKEv2 has two phases: registration and rekeying. In the registration phase a group member contacts the key server to register to a group and receive the policy and keying material needed to talk to the other members and to the key server. The rekeying phase lets the key server renew the keying material for member-to-member communication and for communication with the key server.

There are two ways to register. When a member first contacts a key server it uses the GSA_AUTH exchange, which happens after the IKE_SA_INIT exchange and results in an IKE Security Association between the member and the server. The server authenticates and authorizes the member and then pushes the policy and keys. The second exchange, GSA_REGISTRATION, can be used by the member within the already established IKE SA, for example to register to another group.

Refreshing the group keys is done either in a unicast mode with the GSA_INBAND_REKEY exchange over a specific IKE SA, or in a multicast mode with the GSA_REKEY pseudo-exchange when new keys are distributed to all members. Large groups are likely to use GSA_REKEY for efficiency, while a small group may use GSA_AUTH or GSA_REGISTRATION for registration and GSA_INBAND_REKEY within the same IKE SA. The two can be combined, for example using the more robust inband rekey for the members acting as senders and GSA_REKEY for the rest.

IKEv2 message semantics are preserved, in that all communications consist of message request-response pairs. The exception is the GSA_REKEY pseudo-exchange, which is a single message delivering group updates to the members.
sections.plainLanguage: Some applications send the same traffic to many devices at once, for example a video stream to a group of receivers. Those devices all need the same encryption key. This document defines the protocol that hands out that key and replaces it later.

sections.title: The Roles and the Keys
sections.content:
The document assumes familiarity with the IPsec architecture and its multicast extension, and defines the roles precisely.

A group is a set of IPsec devices that communicate with each other using multicast. A group member is an IPsec device that belongs to a group and is authorized to be a group sender, a group receiver, or both. The Group Controller/Key Server is the server that manages IPsec state for a group: it authenticates members and provides the IPsec SA policy and keying material to them.

Three kinds of security association are involved. A Data-Security SA is a multicast SA between each multicast sender and the group's receivers, and it protects the data between senders and receivers. A Rekey SA is a single multicast SA between the key server and all the members, used for multicast transmission of key management messages. A Group SA is a Data-Security SA or Rekey SA that is shared as part of the group policy. The Group Security Association is the collection of Data-Security SAs and Rekey SAs a member needs in order to receive key updates, and it describes the working policy for the group.

Three kinds of key are named. The Traffic Encryption Key is the symmetric cipher key used in a Data-Security SA to protect traffic. The Key Encryption Key is the symmetric key or set of keys used in a Rekey SA to protect its messages, and may include keys for encryption, authentication and key wrapping. The Key Wrap Key is the symmetric cipher key used to protect another key.

Two delays are defined. The Activation Time Delay says how long group senders should wait after receiving new SAs before sending traffic over them, and the Deactivation Time Delay says how long members should wait after a request to delete Data-Security SAs before actually deleting them. A Sender-ID is a unique identifier of a group sender in the context of an active GSA, used to form the initialization vector in counter-based cipher modes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two roles matter. The key server holds the group's policy and keys. A member is a device that has been let into the group; it may be allowed to send, to receive, or both. Two kinds of shared key are used: one protects the traffic itself, and one protects the messages that carry and replace it.

sections.title: Registering a Member
sections.content:
Initial registration is combined with establishing a secure connection to the key server. It takes at least two exchanges, IKE_SA_INIT and GSA_AUTH, and may take more if an Extensible Authentication Protocol method, a cookie challenge, key exchange method negotiation or IKEv2 intermediate exchanges are used. Each exchange is a request-response pair. IKE_SA_INIT is unchanged from IKEv2: it negotiates the cryptographic algorithms, exchanges nonces and computes a shared key. In addition to the IKEv2 algorithms, a key wrap algorithm is negotiated in this exchange through a new Key Wrap Algorithm transform.

GSA_AUTH is similar to the IKEv2 IKE_AUTH exchange. It authenticates the earlier messages and exchanges identities and certificates. The messages are encrypted and integrity protected with the keys already established, so identities are hidden from eavesdroppers and all fields in all the messages are authenticated. The key server authorizes the member to join the group as part of this exchange, and once it accepts the member it provides the traffic encryption keys and/or a key encryption key in the response.

The member's request carries the Group Identification payload, naming the group it wants to join, and may carry a payload declaring which transforms it is willing to accept. A member that intends to act as a group sender must include a GROUP_SENDER notification, which also lets it ask for Sender-ID values when the Data-Security SA uses a counter-mode cipher. The response carries the group's cryptographic policy in the Group Security Association payload and the key material in the Key Download payload.

If the key server rejects the request, because the group identifier is invalid, authorization fails, or the member cannot support the group's policy, the response carries no policy or keys but a Notify payload with the reason: INVALID_GROUP_ID, AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, REGISTRATION_FAILED or NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN.

Once the IKE SA is up, the member can use GSA_REGISTRATION for further registration requests, for example to join another group, and to report that the policy it was given is unacceptable or that it wants to leave the group. In the latter case the key server must remove the member from the group.
sections.plainLanguage: To join, a device runs the usual IKEv2 handshake with the key server and then sends a request naming the group. The server checks who is asking, decides whether to allow it, and replies with the group's rules and the keys. If it refuses, the reply says why and carries no keys.

sections.title: Rekeying the Group
sections.content:
The key server is responsible for rekeying the group according to the group policy. Rekeying is the operation where the key server provides replacement traffic encryption keys and/or key encryption keys, deletes traffic encryption keys, and/or excludes members. It may start a rekey when the membership or the policy has changed, or when the keys are about to expire. Two kinds of group maintenance channel are provided.

GSA_REKEY is a pseudo-exchange: a single one-way IKEv2 message from the key server that delivers the rekey policy to the members using IP multicast as the transport. It suits large and dynamic groups where policy changes often and a scalable method is needed. Because these messages need no response and go to many members, the IKEv2 windowing mechanism must not be used for them. The header's two SPI fields are treated as a single field of 16 octets holding the SPI of a Rekey SA, and the Message ID starts at the value the key server sent in the GSA_INITIAL_MESSAGE_ID attribute, or at zero if that attribute was not sent, and increases with each new message.

GSA_INBAND_REKEY is a normal IKEv2 exchange over the IKE SA set up for the registration exchange. It gives reliable policy delivery and suits a small group of cooperating devices. The key server may combine the two, for example using the inband exchange for the members acting as senders and GSA_REKEY for the rest.

Deletion of SAs is done with the Delete payload, sent either as part of a GSA_REKEY pseudo-exchange or as a GSA_INBAND_REKEY exchange. A Delete payload with an SPI of zero and a Protocol ID of AH or ESP removes those SAs, and one with an SPI of zero and a Protocol ID of GIKE_UPDATE means the member is excluded from the group. An excluded member must re-register to continue, and it is recommended to wait a randomly chosen time, of the order of seconds, before doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: The key server replaces the group's keys when the membership changes or the old key is about to expire. For a big group it sends one multicast message to everyone. For a small group it sends a separate message to each member over the existing secure connection, which is slower but reliable.

sections.title: The New Payloads
sections.content:
G-IKEv2 is an IKEv2 extension and inherits its wire format, though the processing of some payloads differs. Four new payloads are defined: Group Identification, IDg; Security Association - GM Supported Transforms, SAg; Group Security Association, GSA; and Key Download, KD. The header, the IDg payload and the SAg payload reuse the IKEv2 header, the IDi and IDr payloads and the SA payload respectively. Four new exchange types are added: GSA_AUTH, GSA_REGISTRATION, GSA_REKEY and GSA_INBAND_REKEY.

The G-IKEv2 header uses the same IKE header format as IKEv2, with Major Version 2 and Minor Version 0, and the same fields for the SPIs, the flags, the Message ID and the length.

The Group Identification payload tells the server which group the member wants to join. It is built from the IKEv2 Identification payload; the ID_KEY_ID type must be supported, and the ID_IPV4_ADDR, ID_FQDN, ID_RFC822_ADDR and ID_IPV6_ADDR types should be supported. Its Payload Type is 50.

The GSA payload carries the group's security attributes for the Rekey and Data-Security SAs, and its Payload Type is 51. It holds zero or one Rekey SA policy, zero or more Data-Security SA policies and zero or one group-wide policy, with at least one of the first two present. The first octet of each policy substructure says which kind it is: zero for a group-wide policy, and a Security Protocol Identifier for a group SA policy. A proposal for the rekey channel is identified by the Security Protocol Identifier GIKE_UPDATE with the value 6.

The SAg payload declares which transforms the member is willing to accept and uses the format of the IKEv2 Security Association payload, with Payload Type 33, the same as the SA payload. The Key Download payload carries the group keys for the SAs named in the GSA payload, and its Payload Type is 52.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol adds four new pieces of data to the IKEv2 message format: which group a member wants to join, which algorithms the member can accept, the group's security policy, and the keys themselves. It also adds four new kinds of exchange.

sections.title: Key Wrapping and Access Control
sections.content:
Through the rekey, G-IKEv2 supports algorithms such as the Logical Key Hierarchy, which has the property of denying access to a new group key by a member removed from the group and to an old group key by a member added to it. This is unrelated to the perfect forward secrecy property of IKEv2. Other algorithms with the same properties have been proposed but are not specified here.

All group keys sent to members are encrypted with Key Wrap Keys, and the Key Wrap Algorithm transform says which algorithm is used. Every member knows at least one: the default key wrap key associated with the IKE SA or multicast Rekey SA over which the wrapped keys are sent. For the unicast IKE SA it is computed as the pseudo-random function applied to the derived key and the 20-character string "Key Wrap for G-IKEv2". For the multicast Rekey SA it is provided along with the other SA keys.

For forward access control the server may give each member a personal key wrap key at registration, and may also share intermediate keys among several members to form a hierarchy. The size of a key wrap key is set by the key wrap algorithm, but should not be smaller than the key used for the encryption algorithm of the Rekey SA and of all the Data-Security SAs in the group.

When the membership changes and forward access control is wanted, a rekey message that changes the membership must not carry a new Data-Security SA policy and its keys, because those are not protected with the new key encryption key. A second rekey message can deliver them, because it is protected with the new key. If the policy change must also be hidden from removed members, two sequential rekey messages that each change the key encryption key are needed, because the first one, protected with the current key, still shows the group policy. A rekey message must not change the policy without creating a new key encryption key.
sections.plainLanguage: The keys are never sent in the clear; each is wrapped with another key that the receiver already holds. When a member is removed, the server changes the wrapping key first, so the removed member can no longer learn the new keys, and only then sends the new traffic keys in a second message.

sections.title: Counter-Based Modes and Replay Protection
sections.content:
Several counter-based modes exist for ESP, such as AES-CTR, AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-GMAC, and for AH. These modes require that no two senders in the group ever send a packet with the same initialization vector under the same key and mode. G-IKEv2 meets this in two ways: the key server distributes a unique key for each Data-Security SA, and it assigns each sender a portion of the initialization vector space by giving it one or more unique Sender-ID values.

When the group policy includes a counter-based mode, the key server automatically allocates one Sender-ID to each member acting as a sender on that Data-Security SA, and a member that installs the key in several encryption modules must ask for as many Sender-IDs as it has modules. Sender-IDs are allocated sequentially starting at zero, and each registration by a sender gets fresh values, so the server never has to remember what it handed out before. When the counter reaches its final value, the server must exclude all members, who then re-register and receive new SAs and new Sender-IDs.

The Sender-ID goes into the most significant bits of the initialization vector, in the field whose size is given by the GWP_SENDER_ID_BITS attribute, with the value in the least significant bits and unused bits set to zero. If the value does not fit, the member must treat that as a fatal error and re-register.

IPsec provides an anti-replay service, but with multicast extensions it is not always possible. If several senders share a Data-Security SA, each increments the sequence number in the ESP header independently, so receivers cannot filter out replayed packets. With a single sender it is possible, with restrictions. A new Transform ID, 32-bit Unspecified Numbers, is defined for the Sequence Numbers transform type so that the key server can tell members that sequence number uniqueness is not guaranteed; whether anti-replay is enabled stays a local decision for each member. The key server must include the Sequence Numbers transform in the GSA payload for every Data-Security SA.
sections.plainLanguage: Some encryption modes use a counter that must never repeat, so the server gives each sender its own slice of the counter space. It also warns that when several senders share one key, the receiver cannot tell a replayed packet from a genuine one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When an entity joins the group and becomes a member, it has to trust that the key server only authorized entities that are admitted to the group, and that other members will not leak the information shared within the group.

Registration uses the IKEv2 initial exchanges and inherits all the security considerations documented for IKEv2, covering authentication, confidentiality, on-path attack protection, replay and reflection attack protection and denial-of-service protection. GSA_REGISTRATION gains the same protections. G-IKEv2 also adds the ability to authorize a particular member regardless of whether it holds IKEv2 credentials.

The maintenance channel is cryptographically and integrity protected with the algorithm and key negotiated during registration. The authentication key is distributed at registration and the receiver uses it to check that a rekey message came from the authorized key server. Implicit authentication is also possible, in which the ability to decrypt a message and verify its integrity check value proves the sender knows the group keys and so is a member, but that gives no source origin authentication, so it is not recommended unless the group is small and trusted. Confidentiality comes from a confidentiality key distributed at registration, and the channel is integrity protected with a digital signature.

Each GSA_REKEY message carries a monotonically increasing Message ID. A member recognizes a replayed message by comparing the Message ID with the last one received, and must discard any message whose Message ID is less than or equal to the last received value. Implementations should keep a record of recently received rekey messages for that comparison. The strict separation of roles between the key server and the members, and the restriction that a Rekey SA is inbound or outbound only, also help prevent reflection attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Registration inherits the protections of IKEv2. Rekey messages carry a rising number so a member can drop one that has been replayed, and they are signed so a member knows the message came from the key server and not an impostor.

items.title: No new traffic keys yet
items.text: A rekey that changes membership must not carry new Data-Security SA keys.

items.text: The key encryption key is changed so removed members cannot see the new keys.

items.text: A second rekey, protected with the new key, delivers them.

items.text: A rekey must not change the policy without creating a new key encryption key.
